title: sustained-decode-clock-throttle-and-pcie-link-behavior
body:
Executive summary:

We ran a set of sustained decode runs to surface clock-throttle and PCIe link behavior differences across representative cloud GPU SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S families) and a small matrix of NVIDIA driver + CUDA stacks. The goal was to understand: 1) whether long, sustained token-generation workloads cause measurable GPU clock down-throttling or PCIe link renegotiation that impacts tail latency/throughput; 2) whether specific driver/CUDA combos are more resilient; 3) what operational mitigations (warmup patterns, clock/power overrides, instance selection) matter for production serving.

Bottom line findings (high level):
- On A100 SKUs we see modest (~5-8%) frequency sag after ~10–20 minutes under sustained single-stream decode at max SM utilization with CUDA 11.8 + driver 525. Upgrading driver/CUDA reduced sag to ~2–3%.
- On H100 SKUs frequency remained stable in most driver combos, but one cloud SKU with aggressive power limits showed periodic clock dips correlated with host CPU interrupts and PCIe micro-renegotiations.
- L40S (in our GCP testbed) exhibited unusually stable clocks but a recurrent PCIe link width drop from x16->x8 during NVLink fallback transitions when large KV cache prefetches spilled to host. This link event corresponded to ~12% p99 latency amplification for long contexts.
- Differences are subtle but reproducible: important to measure both GPU clocks and PCIe link state at 1s granularity alongside token-level latency for production-grade SLOs.

Experimental setup (notes):
- Models: llama-2-13b (quantized int8 runtime path), and a 7B decoder-only SFT baseline. Used our standard long-context prefilling pattern: 4k prefill then 2k decode for long-context runs; separate microbench run of 512 prefill + 1k decode for short-context noise baseline.
- Instances tested (representative names): aws-p4d (A100), aws-p5 (H100), gcp-l40s-preview (L40S). Hosts were provisioned in same region for each provider where possible; each run pinned to a fresh VM and cold-started containers to avoid kernel-level caching artifacts across runs.
- Drivers/CUDA tested: driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, driver 535 + CUDA 12.1, driver 545 + CUDA 12.2 (where available on SKU).
- Power/clock policy: default cloud policies unless explicitly set (we did a small subtest with persistence mode + application clocks forced on some A100 runs).
- Observability: nvidia-smi sampling at 1s, nvml poll for sm_clock/mem_clock/power/temperature, ethtool/netlink for PCIe link status where supported, dmesg and host kernel ring buffer for PCIe hotplug events, perf on host for interrupt storms, and per-token timing instrumentation in runtime at 100ms resolution.

Methodology: quick runbook
1) Start VM, set MIG off for A100/H100 runs to get full-gpu behavior.
2) Boot container with runtime and load model weights. Warmup: 50 small batched requests (128 tokens) then wait 90s idle to let driver settle.
3) Run 30-minute sustained decode: prefill 4k + decode in a single request loop at target concurrency=1 (single-stream saturation). Capture all metrics. Repeat 3 times per SKU/driver combo, different random seeds.
4) Run short-context microbenchmark (512 prefill) for 10 minutes as control.
5) Run a variant with forced persistence mode + application clocks where applicable.

Key observations (detailed):
- A100 (aws-p4d):
  - With driver 525 + CUDA 11.8 we saw gradual SM clock descent, starting ~1–2 minutes in and stabilizing after ~12 minutes at ~5–8% below peak clocks. Memory clocks were stable. Power draw remained near TDP but thermal headroom under reported temperature remained ~5–8C.
  - Upgrading to driver 535 + CUDA 12.1 reduced the clock descent magnitude and latency variance; hypothesis: scheduler/firmware fixes in later driver improved sustained clock behavior under continuous kernel occupancy.
  - Forcing application clocks (persistence mode + nvidia-smi -ac) eliminated the descent entirely but increased avg power by ~6% and raised temp by ~3C; p99 latency improved slightly (~3–4% relative). Operational cost/thermal tradeoff noted.
  - We observed no PCIe width drops on A100 runs in our AWS environment.

- H100 (aws-p5):
  - In the default cloud instance we saw stable clocks with both driver 535 and 545. However, one particular provider image (custom host) surfaced periodic micro-dips (~1–2s) in SM clock coincident with host CPU interrupts and kernel tracepoints that appear to be I/O scheduling spikes; these events produced small but visible p99 spikes (~6–10%) in the decode stream when they aligned with decode bursts.
  - We saw one case where a hypervisor-level power capping policy caused more aggressive thermal/power cycling; switching to a host with more permissive power policy removed the dips.
  - NVLink behavior: H100 NVLink transfers were robust; telemetry showed no link width renegotiations during runs.

- L40S (gcp-l40s-preview):
  - Clocks remained stable but PCIe link width logged transient renegotiations: x16->x8 transitions logged at the times when large host-GPU prefetches were issued (simulating KV cache miss recovery). Each renegotiation had ~1–2s duration and correlated with ~10–14% p99 latency amplification for our long-context traces.
  - Hypothesis: firmware/driver on that platform uses a fallback path or power-saving policy when heavy host-GPU DMA occurs; host-side NVMe IO and DMA bursts coincide with serialized PCIe link reconfiguration.
  - Kernel ring buffer occasionally logged messages about hotplug-like link status changes; raising PCIe ASPM to L0 on the host reduced frequency of events in a follow-up run.

Microbench notes and anomalies:
- We saw slight differences between runs depending on container runtime (runc vs. crun); runc runs had marginally higher jitter in some SKUs—likely scheduling interplay with host cgroup/kernel timers. We included runtime as a noise factor in our final ANOVA.
- There were rare 'stutter' events (single token took 2–3x expected time) in one A100 run; looking at kernel logs shows a host-side ADMIN interrupt storm from an unrelated host process. Clean host image runs removed this.

Quantitative snapshot (example numbers, median of 3 runs):
- A100 / driver525 / cuda11.8 / default: avg token throughput 480 t/s, p50 12ms, p95 28ms, p99 52ms (with sustained clock descent: ~6% lower SM clock).
- A100 / driver535 / cuda12.1 / default: avg 498 t/s, p50 11.5ms, p95 26ms, p99 48ms (reduced sag).
- A100 / driver535 / with app-clocks: avg 510 t/s, p50 11.2ms, p95 25ms, p99 46ms (higher power).
- H100 / driver545 / cuda12.2 / default: avg 820 t/s, p50 6.2ms, p95 14ms, p99 28ms (stable clocks); micro-dip events added +6–10% p99 when aligned.
- L40S / driver535 / cuda12.1 / default: avg 620 t/s, p50 8.4ms, p95 19ms, p99 33ms; during PCIe renegotiation windows p99 spiked to ~38ms.

Interpretation and actionable guidance for production:
- Instrument everything at 1s granularity: SM clock, mem clock, PCIe link width, PCIe errors, host IRQ storms, kernel dmesg. These subtle events map to 5–15% p99 impacts and are visible only when correlated with token timings.
- For A100 fleets: prefer newer drivers/CUDA stacks where validated; consider application-clocks for latency-sensitive customers but reserve for dedicated pools because of power/cost implications.
- For H100: pay attention to host selection and cloud images; some host-level policies can induce micro-dips. Target instance types with permissive default power configs for critical low-latency tiers.
- For L40S: test PCIe/ASPM/host NVMe interaction—if your workload does host-GPU DMA bursts (KV prefetch), prefer hosts that allow stable PCIe link policies or adjust prefetch concurrency to reduce link renegotiation.

Open questions and next steps:
- Re-run L40S experiments with firmware upgrade matrix and explicit PCIe ASPM toggles to confirm the host-side mitigation.
- Expand to multi-stream (concurrency>1) experiments to see if clock descent behaves differently under throughput vs. single-stream saturation.
- Add power telemetry from host-level BMC on our dedicated hosts to better attribute power throttling versus host interrupts.
- Draft a short ops playbook for Dedicated customers: how to select instance type + driver combo + whether to enable application clocks.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducibility
- Commands used for sampling: nvidia-smi dmon / nvml poll script (1s), lspci -vvv for link width, ethtool -t (where supported), journalctl -k + dmesg capture. Runtime instrumentation: token timing hooks in runtime binary with flush to local file every 30s.
- Notes-to-self: keep a stable test image that mirrors production runtime stack; random host noise is the single biggest source of flakiness.
